- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slightly.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.33) or volatile, model often underestimates; adjust upward, especially if recent price is falling.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >5% from prior day), model frequently overshoots; cap forecast at 1–2% below peak or use moving average to smooth.
- If model shows strong upward trend but sentiment is weak or mixed, reduce slope; mean-reversion bias is common in 30-day horizon.
- If true outcome is consistently higher than forecast, especially in 30-day window, model underestimates volatility; increase forecast by 0.5–1.5% per day if sentiment is bullish.
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.33–0.67), model often fails to capture mean reversion; use 14-day SMA or 20-day EWMA for smoothing.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, avoid overreacting to short-term sentiment swings; anchor to 18-day moving average unless sentiment is strongly bullish.
- If sentiment is negative and price is rising, model often misreads trend; treat as “reversal” and reduce forecast by 1–2% per day until sentiment stabilizes.
